newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/A few remain cautious on stocks.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/A few remain cautious on stocks.

text.p: U.S. stocks rallied solidy Wednesday, bolstering turnover in major U.S. stock index options, but some options players remained cautious.
By about 1415 CST/1915 GMT, the Dow industrial average was up 79 points at 8,267, just two points off a new session peak.
The S&P 100 index gained 11.47 to 940.80 and the S&P 500 rose 9.64 to 962.01. September S&P 500 futures rallied 9.80 to 966.30.
Chris Cadbury, who publishes a daily market letter, said heavy volumes today suggest the rally could last a few days.

Cadbury explained that Tuesday's New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) volume of 535 million shares was the lightest on a Tuesday since the beginning of July. By late session Wednesday, NYSE volume topped 472 million shares.
"This volume reversal may carry us up for a few days, but I don't see anything very important looming here," he said. "It looks like just a trading rally."
He added that the market is extremely overbought and equity put/call ratios at the American Stock Exchange and Chicago Board Options Exchange are at market-topping levels.
"I don't really see that the market has a great deal left in it here," Cadbury said. "It's really getting to be late in the day."

Jerry Hegarty, an options analyst at Thomson Financial Services in Boston, said in a report that Tuesday's equity put/call ratio of 0.45 at the CBOE was "a serious short term warning signal for stocks."
He noted, however, that index put volume outpaced call volume by 15,000 contracts, which was somewhat bullish.
"When these signals conflict, the result is often choppy action," he said.
In an intraday note, Hegarty said the equity put/call ratio was again in bearish territory, but warned: "it is difficult to ever bet against this bull market."

Jay Shartsis, head of options trading at R.F. Lafferty & Co in New York, agreed that Tuesday's closing equity put/call ratio at the CBOE was pretty low, but said several days of record lows may be needed to signal the market's top.
"There is no precedence," he said. "Everybody is in uncharted water, so maybe you do need records in sentiment."

From a contrarian standpoint, low put/call ratios are generally viewed as bearish because they suggest investors are loading up on calls and passing up on puts, which are often bought for downside protection.
Shartsis noted that well known technical analyst Robert Prechter said in a recent market letter that the current "record-setting optimism" gave few near term market clues.
"This give up of sorts by Prechter, regarding the implications of wild optimism, may mean the end (of the bull run) is close," Shartsis said.
"August can be a fateful month," he added.
